answer.rationale: The hard constraint is no added delivery risk: the primary contract lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew and the line is at 94% with no buffer, so a lapse, deferral, or primary switch would put committed volume at risk. Incumbent already refused a price reopen, so another negotiate cycle is unlikely to clear an 18% cut before expiry and would spend the only decision. c5’s deferral applied to non-critical month-to-month spend, not this cliff. c1 is the continuity case for renewal (stable integration, no migration, deliveries held). c2’s low-cost switch is the TCO temptation but onboarding ‘quick last year’ is unverified against a no-buffer 14-day cutover, so unit-cost savings could be dominated by disruption; treat that as uncertain until the archive is checked. Second-source (c3) does not by itself replace the expiring primary. Renewing the incumbent is the only action that clearly does not increase delivery risk; flag the unmet spend-cut and residual single-source exposure as downstream value risk. Verify c1 and c2 before commit.
